scenario:
Northgate Logistics plc stores and delivers goods for online retailers from five large warehouses in England. Warehouse staff pick and pack orders by hand. Pay is close to the National Living Wage and most staff are on flexible contracts.

Demand for Northgate's services has grown, but its retail customers have complained about late deliveries and picking errors. Two retailers moved their contracts to a rival last year, which uses robots to pick orders.

Northgate's board is considering investing £36m in automated picking systems. The operations director says that this would allow 600 fewer warehouse staff to be employed. The HR director has warned that staff morale is already low.

faster, more reliable picking helps meet delivery deadlines - a key reason customers left
600 fewer staff reduces the impact of high labour turnover and absence
however, the £36m investment increases fixed costs and could reduce flexibility if demand falls; redundancies may damage morale during the transition

In 2024 the value of the pound rose against both the dollar and the euro. Tidewater's export director is concerned that US retailers will turn to cheaper American brands.

Tidewater currently sells to the USA by exporting through an agent. It is considering a joint venture with a US food distributor, which would bottle Tidewater's sauces in the USA under licence.
question: Analyse why Tidewater Foods plc might choose to enter the US market through a joint venture with a US distributor rather than by exporting.

indicative_content: bottling in the USA removes exchange-rate risk on the selling price - important as PED in the USA is -1.8, so the 12.5% dollar price rise could reduce US sales by around 22%
the partner's local knowledge and distribution networks give access to retailers
lower transport costs and shorter supply chains
shared investment and risk compared with building its own US factory
local production may allow responsiveness to US tastes
however, Tidewater would share profits and lose some control over quality and its brand

subject: A-Level Business
topic_title: Strategic methods: how to pursue strategies
scenario:
Background
Priya Nair, an engineer, founded Lumen Bikes Ltd in Sheffield in 2016. Lumen designs and assembles premium electric bikes (e-bikes). Its bikes are lighter than most rivals' and their batteries last longer. Every frame carries a seven-year warranty. Lumen sells directly to customers online and through 40 independent bike shops.

The average Lumen e-bike sells for £2 800, compared with around £1 200 for mass-market e-bikes sold by large retailers. Priya has always said: 'We will never be the cheapest. Our customers pay for quality, design and the knowledge that their bike was built in Britain.'

Demand for e-bikes has grown rapidly as commuters look for alternatives to cars and public transport. Lumen's revenue has risen from £4.1m in 2021 to £14.8m in 2024, and the number of employees has grown from 38 to 112.

Culture and leadership
Priya describes her leadership style as democratic. The structure is flat: there are only three levels of hierarchy. Production teams decide how to organise their own work, and every engineer can spend 10% of their time on their own development projects. Lumen's most successful product, the 'Fold-Go' folding e-bike, began as one engineer's side project. Staff turnover is low and the business regularly wins 'best place to work' awards.

Some managers believe that, as Lumen grows, it will need more formal procedures. Priya disagrees: 'Rules kill ideas.'

Battery supply
Batteries make up 35% of the cost of Lumen's components. Lumen buys all of its batteries from Voltcell Ltd, a specialist supplier in Wales, which also supplies three of Lumen's competitors. In 2024 Voltcell raised its prices by 12%, and late deliveries forced Lumen to stop production for six weeks.

Voltcell's owner is retiring and has offered to sell the business to Lumen for £6.5m.

The decision
Option 1: Lumen buys Voltcell for £6.5m. This would be financed by selling a 30% stake in Lumen to a venture capital firm for £4.5m, with the remaining £2m from a bank loan. Voltcell would continue to supply Lumen's competitors.

Option 2: Lumen signs a five-year supply contract with Hanjin, a large South Korean battery manufacturer. Hanjin's prices would be 8% below Voltcell's current prices and fixed in US dollars for five years. Lead time would be 10 weeks, compared with 2 weeks from Voltcell, and Lumen must order at least 1 500 batteries each quarter.

The cargo bike launch
Lumen plans to launch a new cargo e-bike, designed for families and delivery businesses, in 15 weeks' time. A new production line is needed. The planned activities are shown in Appendix C.
question: Should Lumen Bikes Ltd buy Voltcell (Option 1) or sign the supply contract with Hanjin (Option 2)? Use quantitative and qualitative information to justify your answer.

make a justified recommendation

competitors may stop buying from Voltcell once Lumen owns it - 40% of Voltcell's revenue at risk; Lumen has no experience of battery manufacture; culture clash
Option 2: 10-week lead time means much more inventory and less flexibility; minimum orders reduce flexibility if demand falls
prices fixed in dollars - if the pound falls, costs rise; 'built in Britain' image may be weakened; locked in for 5 years

subject: A-Level Business
topic_title: Strategic methods: how to pursue strategies
scenario:
Background
Tom and Ama Mensah set up GreenRoot Organics Ltd in 2012 on a 120-acre farm in Herefordshire. GreenRoot grows organic vegetables and delivers weekly vegetable boxes to 4 200 subscribers in the West Midlands. Its mission is 'Good food, fairly grown'.

GreenRoot employs 46 people, including 12 adults with learning disabilities who work in its packing shed through a supported-employment scheme. Staff are paid at least the Real Living Wage. Tom and Ama reinvest about 80% of profits in the farm and the local community.

A supermarket contract
A regional supermarket chain has offered GreenRoot a one-year contract to supply 200 tonnes of organic carrots and potatoes. The supermarket would pay 60 days after delivery. GreenRoot's spare land could produce only 150 tonnes; the remaining 50 tonnes would have to come from land currently used to grow vegetables for the boxes.

Growth options
Tom and Ama want GreenRoot to grow so that it can employ more people from the supported-employment scheme. They are considering two options.

Option 1: open three GreenRoot farm shops in nearby towns. This would be financed by raising £600 000 through crowd funding, offering investors 6% interest a year for five years.

Option 2: franchise the GreenRoot veg-box model to other organic farms across the UK. Each franchisee would pay a £20 000 fee and 6% of revenue, and would have to follow GreenRoot's employment and sourcing standards.
question: Would you advise GreenRoot Organics Ltd to choose Option 1 (farm shops) or Option 2 (franchising the veg-box model)? Justify your answer.

mark_scheme.instruction: Levels of response. Determine the level using the descriptors (best fit), then the mark within the level. Indicative content is not exhaustive - credit all valid lines of argument.
demands: analyse both options
make a justified recommendation linked to GreenRoot's objectives

Option 2: rapid national growth using franchisees' capital; fee and 6% of revenue with low risk; spreads the mission through franchisee standards
Option 1: £600 000 debt and the risk of new retail locations; slower growth
Option 2: loss of control - franchisees may not follow employment standards, risking reputation; GreenRoot has no experience of running a franchise; few organic farms may want to join
